clue.text: Writer playing along with EU

indicators.note: An actor playing a part is being somebody other than themselves, and letters told to play will not stay as the clue sets them down.

parts.note: anagram fodder, five letters
the European Union by its usual two initials

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a musician joining in with Brussels, so 'playing' passes as something a person does rather than an instruction to the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Writer → ANGELOU: definition by example — Maya Angelou, the American poet and memoirist who wrote I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings.

clue.text: In which X often appears with a broken leg support

indicators.note: Something broken has come apart and been put back together wrongly, which is what happens to the three letters it sits next to.

parts.note: the clue's own 'a', taken as a single letter
the three letters of LEG, reset in another order
the undergarment is the crossword's standard support

explanation.walkthrough: X is the schoolroom's unknown, so the opening reads as a question about kisses or films. A support that turns out to be underwear is a joke this puzzle never tires of.
explanation.definitionFit: In which X often appears → ALGEBRA: the branch of mathematics that writes unknown quantities as letters, and x is the traditional first choice.

clue.text: Happy soul dancing round Ireland's top flower

indicators.note: A dancer whirling round the floor finishes facing every way but the one they set off in, and so do these letters.

parts.note: glad = happy, and these four letters lead off unshuffled

indicators.note: The top of a word printed down the page is where it starts, so only Ireland's opening letter is wanted.

parts.note: anagram fodder, four letters
the letter Ireland begins with

explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is the word solvers learn to distrust — in a cryptic it is often a river, something that flows — and this time it is honestly a bloom.
explanation.definitionFit: flower → GLADIOLUS: the tall spike of funnel-shaped blooms grown from a corm, named from the Latin for a little sword after its leaves.

clue.text: Was wolf-like lecturer against journalist's opinion piece?

indicators.note: To lean one thing against another is to set them side by side, so this letter simply sits in front of what follows.

parts.note: l = lecturer, the academic abbreviation
an op-ed is the signed column a paper prints opposite its editorial page

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a newsroom quarrel between a lecturer and a journalist, which is why nothing in it suggests an animal crossing open ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Was wolf-like → LOPED: to lope is to run with the long, loose, unhurried stride a wolf covers ground with, so the past tense answers 'was'.

clue.text: Like a single draughts piece — 100 now under review

indicators.note: A review looks at something again and hands it back rearranged, which is what becomes of the nine letters in front of it.

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Under review' looks like one phrase doing one job. Only 'review' is the instruction; 'under' has quietly been handed over as letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Like a single draughts piece → UNCROWNED: in draughts, the British name for checkers, a piece is crowned into a king on reaching the far row.

clue.text: As corsets are spiked all over

parts.note: a drink spiked with spirits has been laced
when time is up it is all over — the sense in 'the game's up'

explanation.walkthrough: The surface dresses every word as one remark about uncomfortable corsetry; both halves of the answer are ordinary idioms wearing that costume.
explanation.definitionFit: As corsets are → LACED UP: a corset closes by threading cord through its eyelets and hauling it tight, which is the everyday phrase for that fastening.

clue.text: Scored, though showing signs of age!

definitions.meaning: to score a surface is to cut or rule straight marks across it
a face that has weathered years is creased and furrowed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Scored' pulls the surface towards football or sheet music, and the exclamation mark sells the sting: one word that can flatter and insult.
explanation.definitionFit: Scored → LINED: a scored surface carries ruled marks and an aged face carries creases, so both senses come back to the same word for a mark.

clue.text: Test player, international, opens another player's electrical store

parts.note: a Test is an international cricket match, and a player who appears in one wins a cap

indicators.note: To open something is to make a gap in it, and the letter named just before slips into that gap.

parts.note: the other kind of player treads the boards, and this word parts after two letters
i = international, the standard abbreviation

explanation.walkthrough: Two kinds of player stand side by side and the surface asks you to read both as sportsmen, which is what keeps the one on the stage out of sight.
explanation.definitionFit: electrical store → CAPACITOR: the circuit component that holds a charge between two plates and gives it back when the circuit needs it.

clue.text: Poet's slowish to drop a name

indicators.note: Dropping something lets it fall away, so the two letters named after this are simply lost from the word.

parts.note: the musical direction for a moderate, walking pace — on the slow side of the tempo markings
the first letter to go is the clue's own 'a'
n = name, the usual abbreviation

explanation.walkthrough: Tempo markings are worth collecting for crosswords, and 'slowish' is doing all the work here: the whole answer is sitting inside one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Poet → DANTE: definition by example — Dante Alighieri, whose Divine Comedy makes him the poet of medieval Florence.

clue.text: Country's introducing a Latin examination

indicators.note: To introduce is to bring something new in — used loosely here, since the letters brought in arrive at the end rather than inside.

parts.note: the South American country with the S of the possessive left on
the clue's own 'a', taken as a letter
l = Latin, as on a school timetable

explanation.walkthrough: The trick is the apostrophe: 'Country's' is not really possessive at all, just a country's name with an S left stuck to it.
explanation.definitionFit: examination → PERUSAL: a perusal is a careful reading right through a document, examining it line by line rather than glancing at it.

clue.text: Master goldsmith's lead file

indicators.note: A lead is what goes in front, so it asks for the letter standing at the front of the word before it.

parts.note: the letter at the head of the word goldsmith
a rasp is a coarse file for wood or metal

explanation.walkthrough: 'Master goldsmith' is a job title in the surface and a seam in the parse — the split falls in the middle of the phrase, which is the whole disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: Master → GRASP: to grasp a subject is to master it, the mental sense of taking firm hold rather than the hand's.

clue.text: Is cricketer able to provide a handy means of access for consumers?

definitions.text: a handy means of access for consumers

parts.note: able to do a thing = can do it
in cricket the opener is the batter who goes in first, at the start of an innings

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark licenses the leap from a sportsman's usefulness to something in the kitchen drawer, and 'handy' does double duty as praise and as description.
explanation.definitionFit: a handy means of access for consumers → CAN-OPENER: the little tool that lets a shopper get at tinned food, so 'access' means opening a tin.

clue.text: You won't see board members taking part in this criminal bloc's NHS fiddle

definitions.text: You won't see board members taking part in this

indicators.note: A criminal breaks the rules and leaves things out of place, which is exactly what befalls the letters that follow.

parts.note: a bloc is a group acting together, plus the S of the possessive
the National Health Service, Britain's state health system, by its initials
a fiddle is a swindle, which is what the surface is describing

explanation.walkthrough: 'Board members' are chessmen rather than directors, and the answer runs on into 12 across. Playing without sight of the board is a real competitive discipline.
explanation.definitionFit: You won’t see board members taking part in this → BLINDFOLD CHESS: the players are given no sight of the board and call their moves from memory.

clue.text: See 11
Ruddy good to get in a depressed state!

indicators.note: Getting in means arriving inside something, so the letter named before it lands within the words that follow.

parts.note: the clue's own 'a', taken as a letter
g = good, the standard abbreviation
a low is a slump — a depressed state of mind or of the market

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruddy' is also the polite British stand-in for a stronger word, which is what the exclamation mark is selling, and the depressed state is a mood, not a country.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruddy → AGLOW: a ruddy face is flushed and warm with colour, which is how a face described as glowing looks.

clue.text: China might be after this line-up — open secret

indicators.note: This is a down clue, so a piece told to go up is read from the bottom of the grid back towards the top.
To open something out is to spread it apart and lay it down differently, so the letters after it need not keep their order.

parts.note: a line is a row, and this one is read upwards
the six letters of SECRET, opened out into another order

explanation.walkthrough: 'Line-up' looks like one word for a squad or an identity parade, and it is two instructions. The city's porcelain works are what make the definition fair.
explanation.definitionFit: China might be after this → WORCESTER: the English cathedral city whose potteries gave Royal Worcester its name, so the china is named after the place.

clue.text: Evening: almost time to collapse

parts.note: nigh is the old word for near — 'the end is nigh'
t = time, as in the physics formulae
a government or a wall that collapses is said to fall

explanation.walkthrough: The colon makes the clue read as a diary note about somebody flagging at the end of the day, while every word after it is quietly supplying letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Evening → NIGHTFALL: the point at which the light goes and darkness arrives, which is what 'evening' names when it means dusk rather than the whole span.

clue.text: Billionaire accepts new car 'hard to break in'

indicators.note: What you accept you take in, so the billionaire's letters open up and receive the ones named next.
Something made new is remade from the same material, so those three letters are rebuilt in a different order.

parts.note: the software billionaire Bill supplies his surname
the three letters of CAR, reordered
h = hard, the grade stamped on a pencil

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'hard to break in' sound like a verdict on a stiff new car. Only the first of those words is wordplay; the rest is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: break in → GATECRASH: turning up at a party nobody invited you to is breaking in on it, and this is the verb for doing exactly that.

clue.text: Maybe Titian or Turner's main form of grinding

indicators.note: A loose anagram signal: it offers the letters that follow as only one possible arrangement, so you may settle them another way.

parts.note: anagram fodder — the painter's name and the little word after it, eight letters

indicators.note: The main letter of a name is its chief one, which is a loose way of asking for the initial and nothing else.

parts.note: the chief, and so the first, letter of Turner

explanation.walkthrough: Two painters side by side make this look like an art quiz, and neither is being defined: one lends his whole name to the letters, the other lends a single one.
explanation.definitionFit: form of grinding → ATTRITION: wearing something down by constant friction, which is what a war of attrition does to an enemy over time.

clue.text: Department head is getting recognition? Rubbish!

indicators.note: The head of anything is its top or its front, so this asks for the letter the previous word starts with.

parts.note: the letter at the front of Department
the clue's own 'is', taken at face value as two letters
credit is the recognition given for work done

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubbish!' at the end reads as the setter's own snort about the department. It is the definition, and it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubbish! → DISCREDIT: 'to rubbish' is British informal for dismissing something as worthless, and destroying its standing is precisely that.

clue.text: Pledge from would-be MP — dregs!

definitions.note: 'Dregs' is plural where the answer is singular: the sediment left in a bottle is spoken of as the dregs, a plural noun naming one settled layer.
definitions.meaning: a parliamentary candidate in Britain must lodge £500, forfeited unless they win a twentieth of the votes cast
what settles out of a liquid and lies at the bottom of the bottle

explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes the two halves read as one weary remark about politics, and both are the same noun: one from the returning officer's desk, one from the bottom of a bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: Pledge from would-be MP → DEPOSIT: the sum a candidate lodges with the returning officer; the same word names what a liquid lets fall, its dregs.

clue.text: Right wants a familiar ex-PM judged

parts.note: r = right, the standard abbreviation
the clue's own 'a', taken as a letter
Edward Heath, prime minister from 1970 to 1974, was known to everyone as Ted

explanation.walkthrough: British prime ministers turn up in crosswords by their familiar first names as often as by their surnames, and 'Right wants' dresses the whole thing as a party dispute.
explanation.definitionFit: judged → RATED: to rate something is to judge its quality and put a value on it, the way a critic rates a film.

clue.text: One's place in Doris's show?

indicators.note: 'In' puts the letters named before it inside the word named after, rather than alongside it.

parts.note: Doris Day, the American singer and film star, supplies the surname
one is the Roman numeral I, and the clue's own 's follows it
pl is the abbreviation for Place in a street address

explanation.walkthrough: 'Doris's show' reads as a programme with her name on it and 'One's place' as somebody's home; neither picture survives the parse.
explanation.definitionFit: show → DISPLAY: a display is a show mounted for people to look at — fireworks, shop windows, temper — and the verbs match too.

clue.text: Police state can't, without a new study of underground movement?

indicators.note: To be without something is to lack it, so the letter named goes missing before anything else is done.
What is made new is made over out of the same material, and these letters are rebuilt into different words.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters
CAN'T gives up its A, leaving three letters for the mix

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a political complaint and the question mark admits the definition is playful — the movement is geological, and the answer runs on into 23 across.
explanation.definitionFit: study of underground movement → PLATE TECTONICS: the geology of how the earth's crustal plates drift, collide and grind past one another far below the surface.

clue.text: Seize one with leader ousted in a new vote

indicators.note: A word's leader is the letter at its front, and ousting throws that letter out of office altogether.

parts.note: the clue's own 'a', taken as a letter

indicators.note: 'In' drops what precedes it inside the little assembly that follows, between its pieces rather than after them.

parts.note: ONE without the letter at its head
n = new, the standard abbreviation
a vote is cast by marking a cross on the ballot paper

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a leadership challenge, so 'leader ousted' reads as political news rather than an instruction to knock a letter off the front of a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Seize → ANNEX: a state that annexes territory seizes it and keeps it, the formal word for taking land by force.

clue.text: See 21
Wrong end of the dish

parts.note: in law a tort is a civil wrong, the injury one person does another

indicators.note: The end of a word is the letter it finishes on, so only the final character of the next word is wanted.

parts.note: the last letter of the word 'the'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrong end of' is an idiom about grasping something the wrong way round, and it splits neatly into a legal noun and one letter of the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: dish → TORTE: a rich, many-layered cake from Germany and Austria, and any prepared item of food can be called a dish.

clue.text: Tender and even more sickly?

parts.note: someone feeling off is out of sorts, and milk that has gone off has turned
the comparative ending -er is what makes a word into more of itself

explanation.walkthrough: This is not a synonym hunt: the back half of the answer is a grammatical ending, and 'even more' is the instruction to add it. Comparatives are a rarer trick than they look.
explanation.definitionFit: Tender → OFFER: a tender is the formal bid a contractor puts in for a job, and to tender something is to offer it.

clue.text: Top grade rations ordered by advanced health centres

indicators.note: Something ordered has been put into an arrangement chosen by somebody else, not the one it arrived in.

parts.note: the top grade awarded in an exam is an A
anagram fodder, seven letters
a = advanced, as in the A-levels taken at eighteen in England and Wales

explanation.walkthrough: Two separate As, one an exam grade and one the advanced level of those same exams, sit either side of the fodder — which is how the letter count reaches nine.
explanation.definitionFit: health centres → SANATORIA: the Latin plural of sanatorium, the residential clinics where patients were sent to convalesce, especially from tuberculosis.

clue.text: Gathering close to Gulf Stream

indicators.note: A close is an ending, so this asks for the letter that finishes the word after it.

parts.note: the final letter of Gulf
a rill is a small stream or brook

explanation.walkthrough: 'Gulf Stream' is one thing in the surface and two instructions in the parse, and the current in the Atlantic has nothing to do with either.
explanation.definitionFit: Gathering → FRILL: in dressmaking a gathering is cloth drawn up on a thread into ruffles, which is exactly what edges a collar or cuff.

clue.text: A cross between tense and loose, as, say, kid's clothing is

indicators.note: What lies between two things has one on either side of it, so these letters take the middle position.

parts.note: t = tense, the grammarian's abbreviation
a cross is the letter X, with the clue's own A in front of it
an animal that is loose has got free of its pen

explanation.walkthrough: 'A cross between' is the everyday phrase for a hybrid, and here it means precisely what it says: a cross, sitting between two other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: as, say, kid’s clothing is → TAX-FREE: children's clothes carry no VAT in Britain, so they are sold free of the tax charged on most goods.

clue.text: Old king protecting (or regressing) fledgling colony

indicators.note: To regress is to go back the way you came, and in an across answer that means reading those letters right to left.
To protect something is to stand all round it, so the king's letters close over what comes next.

parts.note: eight English kings bore the name, which makes it the crossword's default old king
the little word 'or', read backwards

explanation.walkthrough: The brackets make '(or regressing)' look like an editorial aside, which is exactly where two of the letters are hiding.
explanation.definitionFit: fledgling colony → HERONRY: the wood or reed bed where herons nest together season after season, so the colony is full of young birds.
